items.stimulus:
In the summer of 1858 an unusually long spell of hot, dry weather settled over London, and the River Thames began to smell so strongly that newspapers gave the episode a name that has stuck: the Great Stink. The cause was no mystery. For decades the city's growing population had sent its waste into the river, and the problem had worsened as households installed flushing water closets, which emptied into sewers that had originally been built to carry rainwater. Those sewers discharged straight into the Thames, where the tide pushed the waste back and forth past the city instead of carrying it out to sea.

The Houses of Parliament stand on the riverbank, and members found the smell in their committee rooms almost unbearable; curtains soaked in chemicals were hung at the windows in an attempt to mask it. Within weeks, legislation was passed allowing the Metropolitan Board of Works to borrow the money needed for a new drainage system. The Board's chief engineer, Joseph Bazalgette, had already drawn up plans. His scheme relied on large intercepting sewers running roughly parallel to the river, which collected the flow from the older sewers before it reached the Thames and carried it eastwards, mostly by gravity but helped by pumping stations, to outfalls well downstream of the city. Some of the new sewers were laid inside embankments built along the river, which also created new roads.

At the time, most doctors believed that diseases such as cholera were spread by foul air, and the alarm about the smell was driven largely by that belief. A few years earlier the physician John Snow had argued that cholera was carried in contaminated water, but his view was not widely accepted. The new system ended up lending support to Snow. When cholera returned to London in 1866, while parts of the network were still unfinished, the outbreak was concentrated in an area of east London that had not yet been connected. The main works were largely complete by the mid-1870s, and the city suffered no major cholera epidemic after 1866.

items.stimulus:
A conventional prosthetic arm or leg is largely a handmade object. A prosthetist examines the residual limb, takes a plaster cast or measurements, and shapes a socket that must carry the user's weight or the forces of gripping without rubbing the skin raw. The rest of the device is assembled from components that may include joints, cables or, in the most advanced models, battery-powered motors controlled by signals from the user's muscles. The process requires several appointments, and a sophisticated powered arm can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

Three-dimensional printing, which builds an object layer by layer from a digital design, has been promoted as a way to cut both cost and time. Its best-known use so far has been in children's hands. Volunteer networks share free designs online, and anyone with a printer can produce a simple mechanical hand in which bending the wrist pulls on cords that close the fingers. The materials for such a hand are often reported to cost less than a hundred dollars. This matters for children in particular, because they outgrow devices quickly: a conventional limb may need replacing every year or two, whereas a printed hand can simply be reprinted in a larger size.

The limitations are also real. Printed plastic hands are relatively weak and are designed for light tasks such as holding a cup or a ball, not for carrying heavy loads. Many are assembled by volunteers with no clinical training, and a device that fits badly can cause pressure sores or simply be left in a drawer. How many children keep using their printed hands over the long term has not been well studied.

Some clinics are now combining the two approaches. A prosthetist scans the residual limb with a handheld scanner, adjusts the digital model on a computer and prints a trial socket that can be tested and modified within days. Supporters point out that a scan can be stored and reused, but decisions about where the socket should press and where it should relieve pressure still depend on the prosthetist's judgement. In this setting, printing changes how the socket is made rather than who is responsible for making it fit.
items.question: Most children who receive a printed hand stop using it within a year.

items.stimulus:
Suppose you spend a week weighing up a job offer in another city and finally accept it. It seems obvious that the choice was yours and that you could have declined. Determinism challenges this impression. It is the thesis that every event, including every decision, is fixed by earlier states of the world together with the laws of nature. If determinism is true, then given the exact state of the universe long before you were born, your acceptance of the job was the only thing that could have happened.

Philosophers divide sharply over what follows. Incompatibilists hold that genuine freedom requires more than one future to be open at the moment of choice, so that free will and determinism cannot both be true. Some of them conclude that, because determinism or something close to it is true, nobody acts freely; others reject determinism and argue that at least some human choices are not fixed in advance. Compatibilists, by contrast, argue that freedom has never required an open future. On their account, you act freely when your action flows from your own reasons and desires and you are not forced, threatened or manipulated. Your decision about the job meets this standard even if it was causally determined, because it was produced by your own deliberation.

Each side faces a well-known difficulty. Incompatibilists who reject determinism must explain how an undetermined choice would be any more under our control: if nothing settles whether you accept the job, the outcome begins to look like the result of a coin toss inside your head rather than an expression of your character. Compatibilists, meanwhile, are accused of redefining freedom as something too modest. Critics ask why a choice should count as free if its causes stretch back to events over which the chooser had no influence.

It may help to ask what we want freedom for. Much of the debate is driven by concern about responsibility: whether praise, blame and punishment are ever deserved. Disagreements about free will are often, in the end, disagreements about what would have to be true for those practices to be fair.

options.text: more than one future is open to them at the moment of choice.
the action comes from their own reasons and is not coerced.
their decision was not caused by any earlier event at all.
they were able to predict their own decision in advance.

items.stimulus:
Many of the best-known Victorian novels did not first reach readers as books. They appeared in instalments, either in separate monthly parts or as chapters printed weekly or monthly in magazines, and only later were gathered into volumes. Charles Dickens made the format famous in the 1830s, and he later edited weekly magazines of his own in which his novels and those of other writers appeared. In France, novels were serialised in the lower sections of daily newspapers, and in the United States Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin first ran in a weekly anti-slavery paper.

The appeal for publishers was largely economic. A new novel in three volumes was too expensive for most households, and many readers borrowed such books from subscription libraries instead. A magazine instalment, by contrast, cost little, and the price of a whole story was spread over a year or more. A popular serial could also lift a magazine's sales, drawing readers who then paid for the other articles bundled with it.

The format left its mark on the novels themselves. Each instalment needed to hold a reader's interest on its own and to end in a way that made the next one feel necessary, which encouraged dramatic chapter endings, memorable minor characters who could be brought back when interest flagged, and plots with many interwoven strands. Because writers were often only a few instalments ahead of publication, they could respond to readers' letters and to sales figures, expanding a well-liked character or changing direction mid-story. The same pressure could also produce padding, as an author paid by the instalment stretched a thin episode to fill the required space.

Critics who later read these works in single volumes sometimes complained of loose structure and repetition. It is worth remembering that such features were often not flaws of craftsmanship but sensible responses to the way the stories were first read: slowly, over many months, by an audience that might have forgotten earlier details.

A popular serial could also lift a magazine's sales, drawing readers who then paid for the other articles bundled with it.

The format left its mark on the novels themselves. Each instalment needed to hold a reader's interest on its own and to end in a way that made the next one feel necessary, which encouraged dramatic chapter endings, memorable minor characters who could be brought back when interest flagged, and plots with many interwoven strands. Because writers were often only a few instalments ahead of publication, they could respond to readers' letters and to sales figures, expanding a well-liked character or changing direction mid-story. The same pressure could also produce padding, as an author paid by the instalment stretched a thin episode to fill the required space.

Critics who later read these works in single volumes sometimes complained of loose structure and repetition. It is worth remembering that such features were often not flaws of craftsmanship but sensible responses to the way the stories were first read: slowly, over many months, by an audience that might have forgotten earlier details.

items.stimulus:
Intelligence tests are scored against a reference group, and the scale is set so that the average performance of that group equals 100. Because performance drifts over time, publishers periodically re-standardise their tests on new samples so that the average remains at 100. Most test-takers never notice this, because each new edition simply reports results on the familiar scale. In the 1980s the political scientist James Flynn compiled data from many countries showing what this routine adjustment had been hiding: measured against the original norms, scores had risen substantially from one generation to the next, often by around three points per decade. They were largest on tests of abstract reasoning, such as finding the rule that links a series of shapes, and much smaller on tests of vocabulary, general knowledge and arithmetic. The rise was also too rapid to be explained by genetic change, which led researchers to look for environmental causes. Candidates include better nutrition and health, longer and more demanding schooling, smaller families, and daily lives that increasingly call for classification and hypothetical thinking.

Since the 1990s, data from several countries, including Norway and Denmark, have shown the gains slowing, stopping or even reversing slightly. This change has been interpreted in different ways, and no single explanation has been agreed. It does show, however, that the earlier rise was not an unstoppable trend.

items.stimulus:
Regulators often have to decide what to do about a possible hazard before the science is settled. A new chemical may be suspected of harming wildlife, or a new technology of affecting health, while studies remain few or contradictory. The precautionary principle is meant as a guide for such situations. In its most widely cited international form, adopted at a United Nations conference in 1992, it states that when serious or irreversible environmental damage is threatened, a lack of complete scientific proof should not justify delaying cost-effective preventive action. The European Union has since written the principle into its founding treaties as a basis for environmental policy.

That formulation is modest. It does not say that every uncertain risk must be banned; it says only that uncertainty is not, by itself, a sufficient excuse for doing nothing. Stronger versions, sometimes proposed by campaigners, place the burden on anyone introducing a new product or activity to show that it is safe before it is allowed. Critics argue that these stronger versions are incoherent, because inaction also carries risks. Banning a pesticide, for example, may lead farmers to switch to an older and more harmful substitute, or may reduce harvests. If every option might cause harm, a rule that forbids any option that might cause harm forbids everything.

This criticism is fair against the strongest versions, but it does not dispose of the principle. Used well, precaution is a way of setting priorities rather than a veto. It asks regulators to take seriously harms that would be severe or hard to reverse, to compare the risks of acting with the risks of waiting, to choose measures proportionate to the threat, and to revisit the decision as evidence accumulates. A temporary restriction that is lifted when reassuring evidence arrives is not a failure of the principle but an example of it working as intended.

items.stimulus:
Most historians trace chess to a game called chaturanga, played in northern India by around the sixth century CE. Its name referred to the four divisions of an ancient army, namely infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots, and these were represented by pieces that are recognisable ancestors of the modern pawn, knight, bishop and rook. The game was played on a board of eight squares by eight, and its central aim was to trap the opposing king rather than simply to capture pieces.

From India the game travelled to Persia, where it became known as chatrang, and after the Arab conquest of Persia in the seventh century it spread through the Islamic world under the name shatranj. Players in Baghdad and elsewhere wrote treatises analysing openings and endgame positions, and several familiar terms date from this period. The word checkmate is usually traced to a Persian expression announcing that the king is helpless, and rook comes from the Persian name for the chariot.

Chess probably reached Europe by around the year 1000, through Muslim Spain and through trading links with Italy. For several centuries the European game remained much like shatranj, and it was slow. The piece standing beside the king, an adviser in the Persian game, which Europeans came to call the queen, could move only a single square diagonally, and the elephant, ancestor of the bishop, could only jump two squares diagonally. Games could drag on for hours with little decisive action.

In the late fifteenth century, players in southern Europe adopted new rules that allowed the queen to move any distance in a straight line and the bishop to travel any distance along a diagonal. The changes made attacks far more dangerous and games much quicker to decide. The new form spread rapidly, helped by the appearance of printed chess books, and within a few generations it had largely replaced the older game across Europe.

The store accepts a small loss, or no profit, on them in the expectation that customers drawn in by the bargain will fill their trolleys with other goods carrying healthier margins.

The choice of item matters. A loss leader works best when it is something people buy often and whose usual price they remember, so that a cut is noticed and talked about. Stores also tend to place everyday staples towards the back of the shop, which means that a customer who comes in only for the discounted milk must walk past many other products to reach it. Whether this layout is designed to tempt or simply reflects where refrigeration is easiest to install is debated, but its effect on the shopper's route is the same either way.

The strategy has risks. Some shoppers, sometimes called cherry-pickers, visit several stores and buy only the discounted items in each, leaving the retailer with the losses but none of the hoped-for extra sales. Stores respond by limiting the number of discounted items each customer may buy. Manufacturers of branded goods may also object when their products are used as loss leaders, fearing that a very low price will lead shoppers to see the brand as cheap.

Governments have taken different views. Several countries, France among them, have long prohibited retailers from reselling goods below the price they paid, while others allow it unless it is part of a deliberate attempt to drive competitors out of the market. Supporters of such bans argue that large chains can absorb losses that small shops cannot; opponents reply that the bans keep prices higher for consumers.
